canonicalExplanation.summary: **Landmark** elements mark the big regions of a page so assistive technology can jump straight to them: `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>` (exactly **one** visible), `<aside>`, `<footer>`, and labelled `<section>`s. When a page has two of the same landmark (two navs), give each an `aria-label` so users can tell them apart. Plain `<div>` is still right for pure layout wrappers.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A screen-reader user lands on your course page and asks for the list of landmarks. They hear "navigation, navigation, main" — which nav is the site menu and which is the topic list? A page has one main content region and labels two nav regions as Primary and Course topics. In this lesson you'll structure a page with one clear main region and meaningful labeled navigation and sections.

sections.heading: Label duplicates

includes: Use header, nav, main, aside, footer and labelled section appropriately.
Label repeated landmarks and keep div for pure layout.
excludes: ARIA landmark roles written by hand.

outcomes: Structure a page with one clear main region and meaningful labeled navigation and sections.

examples.title: One main and two labelled navs
examples.situation: A page has one main content region and labels two nav regions as Primary and Course topics.
walkthrough: **One main content region:** everything unique to this page sits inside a single `<main>`.
**Labels two nav regions:** `aria-label="Primary"` on the site menu and `aria-label="Course topics"` on the in-page list.
**Check:** the browser's accessibility tree will show banner, navigation "Primary", main, navigation "Course topics", contentinfo.
examples.result: Screen-reader users can jump to the main content or the right navigation by name.

examples.title: The landmark overload
examples.situation: A developer turns every div into a section, including card grids and spacing wrappers, and adds a main inside each article.
walkthrough: Dozens of unnamed regions and several mains make the landmark list noisy and confusing.
Layout wrappers carry no meaning, so they shouldn't be landmarks.
Fix: one main; sections only for headed, themed content; div for layout.
examples.result: The landmark list shrinks to a handful of meaningful regions.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Every div should be replaced with a landmark element to maximize accessibility.
misconceptions.correction: Landmarks help only when they mark genuinely distinct regions; too many make navigation harder. Use one main, labelled duplicates, sections for headed themed content, and div for layout.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The landmark overload", why did more landmarks make the page harder to use?

analogy.example: Landmarks are like **signs in a shopping mall**: Entrance, Food Court, Main Hall, Exit. Two signs both saying "Shops" need extra words ("Shops — Level 1") to be useful. A sign on every pillar helps no one.
limitations: Mall signs are visual; landmarks are mostly used by assistive tech.
Pillars (divs) hold the building up without needing signs.

steps.explanation: The first nav region is labelled Primary.
The page has one main content region.
The second nav is labelled Course topics, so the two are distinguishable.

trace.textAlternative: Landmarks on a course page. Step 1, Site navigation: landmark is navigation; name is Primary. The first nav region is labelled Primary. Step 2, Main region: landmark is main; count is 1. The page has one main content region. Step 3, Topic navigation: landmark is navigation; name is Course topics. The second nav is labelled Course topics, so the two are distinguishable.

faded.prompt: For "One main and two labelled navs", explain why the page has one main content region and how it labels two nav regions as Primary and Course topics.

nearTransfer.prompt: Sketch the landmarks for a blog post page with a site header, the article, a "Related posts" sidebar, and a footer with links.
expectedEvidence: header, main containing the article, aside labelled Related posts, footer.
Footer links in a labelled nav if they're a menu.

farTransfer.prompt: Open a site you use daily with a screen reader's landmark list (or DevTools accessibility tree). List its landmarks and suggest two improvements.

remediation.explanation: Ask of each wrapper: **Is this a major region someone would want to jump to?** Yes → landmark (label it if its type repeats). No → div.

recap.summary: To structure a page with landmarks, use header, nav, one main, aside, footer and headed sections for real regions, label repeated landmarks like two navs, and keep div for layout-only wrappers.
